summary: Light on a two-mile shoal in San Francisco Bay, 1905 to 1960: a square dwelling on eleven cylinders; its upper stories were barged to Tinsley Island in 1966.

structures.note: Eleven foundation cylinders carrying a platform, with a square two-story dwelling and a cylindrical lantern; the top two stories were moved to Tinsley Island (LighthouseFriends text gives July 1966; its photo caption gives 1960).

access.note: Owned by the St. Francis Yacht Club. Grounds, dwelling and tower closed; landing on Tinsley Island needs permission (LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: The lens is at the Angel Island museum; the pilings are visible from the Vallejo-San Francisco ferry.

stay.note: Used by St. Francis Yacht Club members and guests; access is typically limited to guests staying in the house (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: St. Francis Yacht Club (owner of the relocated house)

events.note: Station built on eleven foundation cylinders; Notice to Mariners announced a light 52 ft above the water
Fixed white lens-lantern light announced for about 28 December 1905 (Notice to Mariners, as LighthouseFriends quotes it)
The earthquake tilted the support cylinders as much as eleven degrees eastward; the station was re-leveled and braced
Fifth-order lens replaced the lens lantern, March 1911 (LighthouseFriends)
Fog bell changed from bell operated by machinery to air diaphone
Keeper A. H. Joost assisted a disabled launch in a fog, 21 November (year from the 1925 Bulletin volume)
Assistant keeper Max Schlederer rescued two men in a disabled motor boat, 11 August (year from the 1928 Bulletin volume)
Keeper Albert H. Joost burned in a gasoline flash while relighting a blowtorch used on a radio aerial, 23 December; died 25 December
St. Francis Yacht Club purchased Tinsley Island, where the upper stories were later moved
Manned station no longer required; the light was discontinued

Top two stories lifted off the pilings in July and barged up the delta to Tinsley Island (LighthouseFriends text; its photo caption gives 1960, and Wikipedia's lead gives 1960 for this move; not resolved)

corrections.why: The record's point is the relocated house on Tinsley Island in the San Joaquin Delta (LighthouseFriends). The station stood on Southampton Shoal in San Francisco Bay, between Richmond and Angel Island; the archive's position is 37 deg 52' 49" N, 122 deg 24' 02" W. The record's ENC point is 37.88194, -122.40023.
The archive gives the light 52.5 feet (16.0 m) above mean high water; the 1905 Notice to Mariners, as LighthouseFriends quotes it, says 52 feet. The record's 9.8 m does not match either.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata and Rowlett's directory give a second tower built and first lit in 1960. The archive gives 1905 as establishment, and LighthouseFriends describes one house, manned until 1960, with a red light on a pole there today. The 1960 'tower 2' may be that later light, but no source dates it. Not confirmed.

The archive lists a fifth-order Fresnel as the original optic installed in 1905. LighthouseFriends says the first light was a lens lantern and that a fifth-order lens replaced it in March 1911. The story gives both.

The archive prints the county as San Joaquin and the town as Stockton, which fit the relocated house on Tinsley Island rather than the shoal. The record's Contra Costa is also unsettled, because the shoal lies in the bay between Richmond and Angel Island.

notes_for_editor: Location: the record's point is the relocated house on Tinsley Island (delta); the station's own site is on Southampton Shoal in SF Bay. The roster matched by name with a warning (the archive's position is 81 km from the record's point); the place page's coordinates are the shoal. The archive's county (San Joaquin) and town (Stockton) are the relocation's, not the shoal's. Dates: LighthouseFriends gives July 1966 for lifting the top stories; Wikipedia (lead only, not cited) gives 1960. Not resolved. Names: the archive lists John O. Lunden (1929-1930) and LighthouseFriends calls the assistant Ole Lunden; the story says the archive does not connect them. 1935 fire: the year and the flame details come from LighthouseFriends; the Bulletin (1936) gives the dates without the year. Chronicling America searches for Joost in CA 1935-36 found nothing. 1925 and 1928 Bulletin rescues: the passages read give month and day only; the years are the Bulletin issues'. The 1900 Board report names a ship under tow; the OCR reads 'Maulsden' and the story does not use the name. The Board's reports for 1906-1911 are not in the local corpus (it holds Board reports to 1901), so the 1906 earthquake and 1911 lens come from LighthouseFriends alone. The roster includes USCG names printed 'at least 1950', as the archive prints them; they are not described in prose. Chronicling America searches for Southampton Shoal in CA 1903-12 returned nothing usable. The 1905 Notice to Mariners is known only through LighthouseFriends' quotation of it. Verification pass 2026-10-28: the 1900 Board passage that the story first called a fog signal 'at the point' concerns Quarry Point on Angel Island, not the shoal, and is now worded so. The 1900 Board's 'enormous' is read from OCR that prints 'ekormous' (the word is also in LighthouseFriends' transcription); the Board's own page is cited for the passage, and the quote check runs against the OCR's clean wording. The 1901 $30,000 item was matched on the same OCR line as its label, so it was read by line position, not by column; the image was not opened. The 1936 Bulletin gives Joost and his wife putting out the fire together, which the story now follows. LighthouseFriends' photo caption 'Lighthouse being lifted from its foundation in 1960' conflicts with its text (July 1966); the story states the conflict. The roster matches roster.py output exactly (53 lines, including person slugs); it was matched by name only, with the 81 km warning, and the place page's coordinates are the shoal's.
